questions.question:
**In the following question, some part of the sentence may have errors. Find out which part of the sentence has an error and select the appropriate option. If a sentence is free from errors, select 'No Error'.** 

She is walking (1)/ in the park (2)/ since morning. (3)/ No error (4)
questions.solution:
The correct answer is **1**, i.e., *'She is walking'*

* [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__***

__
 
• It is clear through the word '**since'** that the walking began in the morning and is still ongoing.
 
• In such cases, **present perfect continuous tense** is used since it is an action that is continuing in the present.

**Thus the correct sentence is: ***She has been walking in the park since morning.*

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• Please refer to the following table for the types of tenses and their uses
 
 
 

 **Tense**
 **Functions**
 **Example**
 
 

 Present simple
 used for facts, generalizations, and truths that are not affected by the passage of time
 “She **writes **a lot of papers for her classes.”
 
 

 Past simple
 used for events completed in the past
 “She **wrote** the papers for all of her classes last month.”
 
 

 Future simple
 used for events to be completed in the future
 “She **will write** papers for her classes next semester.”
 
 

 Present perfect
 used to describe events that began in the past and are expected to continue, or to emphasize the relevance of past events to the present moment
 “She **has written** papers for most of her classes, but she still has some papers left to write.”
 
 

 Past perfect
 used to describe events that happened prior to other events in the past
 “She **had written** several papers for her classes before she switched universities.”
 
 

 Future perfect
 used to describe events that will be completed between now and a specific point in the future
 “She **will have written** many papers for her classes by the end of the semester.”
 
 

 Present continuous
 used to describe currently ongoing (usually temporary) actions
 “She **is writing** a paper for her class.”
 
 

 Past continuous
 used to describe ongoing past events, often in relation to the occurrence of another event
 “She **was writing** a paper for her class when her pencil broke.”
 
 

 Future continuous
 used to describe future events that are expected to continue over a period of time
 “She **will be writing** a lot of papers for her classes next year.”
 
 

 Present perfect continuous
 used to describe events that started in the past and continue into the present or were recently completed, emphasizing their relevance to the present moment
 “She **has been writing** a paper all night, and now she needs to get some sleep.”
 
 

 Past perfect continuous
 used to describe events that began, continued, and ended in the past, emphasizing their relevance to a past moment
 “She **had been writing **a paper all night, and she needed to get some sleep.”
 
 

 Future perfect continuous
 used to describe events that will continue up until a point in the future, emphasizing their expected duration
 “She **will have been writing** this paper for three months when she hands it in.”

questions.question:
**In the following question, the sentence given with blank to be filled in with an appropriate word. Select the correct alternative out of the four and indicate it by**** ****selecting the appropriate option.** 

He was sorry ______ her loss.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is **for**

** [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__**

 
• The sentence intends to convey that**: **He felt sorry** because she suffered a loss **and thus, he is trying to empathize with her.
 
• **'about' **means with respect to
 
• **'at' **generally means focusing on a fact or looking *at *something
 
• **'from' **is not a grammatically-right fit here
 
• **'for' **is used to indicate the reason behind something; it is used as a function word to indicate the object or recipient of perception, desire, or activity

**Thus the correct sentence is: ***He was sorry for her loss*

questions.question: **Rearrange the parts of the sentence in the correct order.** It is up to
questions.solution:
The correct answer is **PRQ**

** [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__**

 
• The first sentence ends with "**up to"**. Hence the next sentence should begin with a living noun, i.e., **"consumers" **as mentioned in statement part **P.**
 
• According to **'P', **consumers can appreciate something but if we continue with statement part **Q,** "appreciate exercise with power..." is grammatically wrong as two main verbs cannot exist successively
 
• However, **hence consumers can appreciate the threat of antibiotic resistance... **is meaningful because the subject (*consumers*) is doing some action (verb - *appreciate*) with the object (*t**hreat*)
 
• The sensible flow of passage should be from the cause of appreciation to the object of appreciation and finally to the method of handling that appreciation

**Hence, the correct answer is: ***It is up to the consumers now to appreciate the threat of antibiotic resistance and exercise this power with care.*

questions.question:
**A sentence has been given in Direct/Indirect Speech. Out of the four given alternatives, select the one which best expresses the same sentence in**** ****Indirect/Direct Speech.** 

“Are you going to eat with us?” he asked.

options.text: He asked me if I was going to eat with them.
He asked whether he was going to eat with them.
He inquired whether I am going to eat or not.
She asked me if he was going to eat with them.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is **He asked me if I was going to eat with them. **

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

To change the sentence from **Direct** to **Indirect **we should:

 
• Make changes in tenses of reported speech only when the reporting verb is in the past tense.
 
• When the reported speech is an interrogative sentence we follow these steps-
 
 
• The reporting verb 'said' is changed into 'asked'.
 
• Connector 'if' or 'whether' is used in place of commas.
 
• Change the sentence, given in the reported speech, from interrogative to assertive.
 
• The tense of reported speech is changed accordingly.(in above sentence- 'are' changes into 'was')
 
• Personal Pronouns of reported speech are changed as per the subject and object of reporting verb. Here, the second person- 'You' will change into **'I'** as per object - **'me' (hidden).**
 
 

**Thus the correct answer is Option 1**

• Thus, the blank should be filled with a **noun**
 
• Among the given options, ***'compensate',*** ***'to compensate' ***and ***'compensating' ***are **verbs; **only ***'compensation' ***is a **noun**
 
• ***Compensation*** means ***'money that you pay to somebody because you have injured him/her or lost or damaged his/her property'***
